name: smollm2.c — maximize decode tok/s vs Ollama

description: Baseline: NEON F16 matmul 4-acc unroll-16, clang -O2 -march=native

asi.hypothesis: baseline measurement
asi.ollama_output: I'm doing great! How can I help you today?
asi.bottleneck: matmul() called 210x per decode step, logit projection 49152x576 F32 also hot

description: -O3 -ffast-math: no improvement over -O2, within noise

asi.hypothesis: -O3 -ffast-math would improve throughput via auto-vectorization and fast math
asi.result: 27.0 vs baseline 27.8, within noise, not a real improvement
asi.rollback_reason: no gain, compiler already vectorizing well at -O2 with NEON intrinsics
asi.next_action_hint: Compiler flags exhausted. Focus on algorithmic: precompute RoPE sin/cos table, or 8-accumulator matmul, or F16 KV cache

description: Precompute RoPE sin/cos table: no improvement, within noise

asi.hypothesis: RoPE powf/cosf/sinf per step was a bottleneck, precompute to save compute
asi.result: 27.3 vs baseline 27.8 — within noise, no gain
asi.rollback_reason: RoPE was not the bottleneck. head_dim=64, n_heads=9, only 32 trig calls per token per layer — trivial vs matmul cost
asi.next_action_hint: matmul is the real bottleneck: 210 calls/step. Try 8-accumulator matmul or unroll-32 to improve NEON throughput. Also try F32 logit projection with NEON (currently matmul_f32 uses 2-acc unroll-8, could do 4-acc unroll-16)

description: 2-row matmul tiling: slower (20.4 vs 27.8), register pressure hurts

asi.hypothesis: process 2 output rows simultaneously with 8 accumulators to hide FMA latency and better utilize NEON
asi.result: 20.4 vs baseline 27.8 — significantly WORSE. 8 acc per output pair = too much register pressure on ARM64 (32 SIMD regs total, 8 float32x4 = 8 regs, x-vectors reloaded = cache thrash)
asi.rollback_reason: register spill and x-vector reload overhead outweigh FMA latency hiding
asi.next_action_hint: Single-row with 4 acc is optimal for this CPU. Try unroll-32 (2x the inner loop) to reduce loop overhead. Or try dot-product trick: vdotq_... not applicable for F32. Try vld1q_f16 + vcvtq_f32_f16 instead of vld1_f16+vcvt_f32_f16 to load 8 F16 at once. Also try matmul_f32 NEON upgrade (logit proj).

description: unroll-32 with vld1q_f16 + vget_low/high: slower than unroll-16 baseline

asi.hypothesis: wider loads (vld1q_f16 8 elements) and unroll-32 would reduce loop overhead and improve throughput
asi.result: 24.9 vs baseline 27.8 — slower. 8 accumulators per row = register pressure even in single-row case
asi.rollback_reason: 8 acc regs + 8 weight regs + x reloads = too much for ARM64 register file in single row. Original 4-acc unroll-16 is the sweet spot for this workload.
asi.next_action_hint: matmul inner loop already at sweet spot with 4-acc unroll-16. Focus elsewhere: (1) matmul_f32 logit projection is pure F32 49152x576 — try NEON with vld1q_f16 on x (currently F32), (2) attention inner loop (QK dot + softmax + weighted sum) — NEON vectorize, (3) SwiGLU loop — NEON sigmoid. (4) Try batching/prefetch hints __builtin_prefetch.

description: matmul_f32 logit projection: 4-acc unroll-16 (was 2-acc unroll-8)

asi.hypothesis: logit projection 49152x576 F32 was underutilizing NEON with 2-acc unroll-8, 4-acc unroll-16 better hides FMA latency
asi.result: 28.3 vs baseline 27.8 — small but positive improvement (+0.5 tok/s)
asi.confidence: low, may be within noise, will re-run to confirm

description: Re-run confirm: matmul_f32 4-acc change is within noise (27.5 vs 27.8 baseline)

asi.hypothesis: confirming previous keep of matmul_f32 4-acc
asi.result: 27.5 on re-run vs 28.3 first run vs 27.8 baseline — variance too high, no real gain
asi.rollback_reason: improvement was noise. Reverting to baseline.
asi.next_action_hint: Look at the attention inner loop (QK dot + value accumulation). Currently scalar float loops. Try NEON vectorization there. Also try SwiGLU sigmoid with NEON. Consider if there's a way to avoid recomputing full attention on every decode step.

description: NEON attention QK dot + value acc + residual adds: noisy, avg ~27.7, not a clear win

asi.hypothesis: vectorize QK dot product, value accumulation, and residual adds with NEON to reduce scalar overhead
asi.result: 3 runs: 28.5, 28.2, 26.5. Average ~27.7, baseline 27.8. High variance, no real gain.
asi.rollback_reason: SwiGLU NEON path is actually slower due to scalar-loop-in-NEON disguise (store/load to temp array then scalar expf). Residual adds are memory-bound not compute-bound. QK dot gain masked by variance.
asi.next_action_hint: Attention inner loop gains are marginal due to short hd=64 vectors. Focus on biggest flop blocks: ffn gate/up matmul [1536x576], down [576x1536] which run 30x per step. Try __builtin_prefetch for weight rows. Or try rmsnorm NEON (30x per step). Or profile to find true bottleneck.

description: F16 logit projection: use w_token_embd_f16 (F16) instead of F32 for tied embedding logit proj — halves memory bandwidth for 49152x576 matmul

asi.hypothesis: logit projection is 18.9% of decode step. Using F16 weights halves memory bandwidth for this 49152x576 matmul (270MB/s saved), using existing NEON F16 matmul path
asi.result: 3 runs: 28.8, 29.9, 28.2. Median 28.8. Baseline 27.8. +1 tok/s improvement. Consistent positive.
asi.memory_note: adds 49152*576*2 = 56.6MB F16 copy of w_token_embd in memory, was F32 only before

description: NEON rmsnorm: within noise (26.8, 28.0 vs baseline 28.8 new baseline)

asi.hypothesis: NEON vectorize rmsnorm (called 60x per decode step: 30 attn + 30 ffn) to reduce scalar loop overhead
asi.result: 26.8 and 28.0 — avg 27.4, below new baseline 28.8. RMSnorm is memory-bound for dim=576, scalar vs NEON doesn't matter much
asi.rollback_reason: rmsnorm cost is dominated by sqrtf/inverse, not the loops themselves. dim=576 is small enough the scalar loop is already fast.
asi.next_action_hint: Focus on memory bandwidth: the main matmul is 210 calls per step over ~130MB of weights total. Try prefetch hints for weight rows to pipeline memory access. Or try quantizing KV cache to F16 to reduce memory bandwidth for attention. Or try avoiding the double decode of x in rmsnorm (compute in-place).

description: prefetch next weight row: slower (25.7, 27.5) vs baseline 28.8, prefetch distance too short or OS already prefetches

asi.hypothesis: __builtin_prefetch 2 rows ahead to overlap L2 miss latency for weight access in matmul
asi.result: 25.7, 27.5 — worse than baseline 28.8. Prefetch with distance=2 is too short, creates cache contention.
asi.rollback_reason: the OS/HW prefetcher on this Snapdragon likely already handles sequential access. Adding software prefetch creates contention.
asi.next_action_hint: Software prefetch ineffective here. Try larger prefetch distance (4-8 rows) as separate experiment, or skip. Consider: can we reduce total weight bytes loaded? KV cache F16 compression would save attention bandwidth. Try F16 KV cache (pack k/v as F16 to halve bandwidth in attention).

description: F16 KV cache: slower (24.7, 25.4) vs baseline 28.8 — F16 decode in attention inner loop costs more than bandwidth saved

asi.hypothesis: F16 KV cache halves memory bandwidth for attention (kv_dim=192, pos=50 tokens → ~19KB saved per step), enabling faster attention
asi.result: 24.7, 25.4 — significantly worse than baseline 28.8. The KV cache is tiny (30 layers * 50 pos * 192 dim * 4B = 1.1MB F32) — fits in L2/L3 cache entirely. F16 decode overhead (vcvt per element in QK dot + value accum) adds cost with no bandwidth benefit when data is already cached.
asi.rollback_reason: KV cache is small enough to be L2-cached. F32→F16→F32 round-trip adds latency with no memory bandwidth benefit.
asi.next_action_hint: KV cache compression not beneficial here. The weights are the bottleneck, not KV cache. Attention itself is a tiny fraction of compute vs matmul. Focus on: (1) try -O3 specifically for forward.c only, (2) try loop unrolling of matmul inner loop with pragma, (3) try aligning weight arrays to 64B for better cache line utilization, (4) measure Ollama actual tok/s and compare properly.

description: -O3 for forward.c only: slower than -O2 (25.4 vs 28.8)

asi.hypothesis: -O3 might auto-vectorize loops better than -O2 when applied only to the hot forward.c file
asi.result: 25.4 vs baseline 28.8. Worse. -O3 may unroll loops in ways that thrash icache, or miscompile NEON intrinsics.
asi.rollback_reason: -O2 with manual NEON intrinsics outperforms -O3 auto-vectorization for this workload
asi.next_action_hint: Compiler path exhausted. Think differently: (1) Reduce number of matmul calls — currently q/k/v are separate, could fuse into one [q+k+v] * x matmul. For decode step, dim=576, q=576, k=192, v=192 = 960 outputs. Fused = 1 loop over x instead of 3. (2) Fuse gate+up FFN matmul similarly. (3) Measure actual time per matmul call with perf counters if possible.

description: qkv_buf + matmul_qkv prep (no actual fusing yet): within noise, no gain

asi.hypothesis: prep for fused QKV: added qkv_buf allocation and matmul_qkv wrapper. No actual loop fusion implemented yet.
asi.result: 26.7 vs baseline 28.8 — slightly worse within noise. No change to hot path.
asi.rollback_reason: no improvement, reverting. True QKV fusion requires single loop over x computing q/k/v rows together — complex and risky for marginal gain given each matmul already independently vectorized.
asi.next_action_hint: QKV fusion is complex for small gain. Different angle: measure if the benchmark itself is noisy due to CPU freq scaling. Try pinning to performance cores or running under taskset. Also: profile with perf stat to get actual cycle counts and cache miss rates. Or try a completely different approach: implement BLAS-like blocked matrix multiplication to improve cache utilization.

description: Re-baseline with warmup: steady-state is 24.5 tok/s (not 28.8 which was burst freq)

asi.hypothesis: establish true steady-state baseline after CPU frequency throttling characterization
asi.result: True steady-state: ~24.5 tok/s. Earlier 28.8 was burst CPU freq on first run. The F16 logit proj improvement is still kept as it was real (+1 tok/s vs true F32 baseline ~23-24).
asi.benchmark_insight: CPU throttles after ~2 runs from 3GHz to ~2.4GHz sustained. Warmup 2 runs before measuring captures steady-state. Noise floor now ~1 tok/s.
asi.ollama_comparison: Ollama steady-state: 13.7 tok/s. We are 1.8x faster.

description: pthread thread pool for matmul: catastrophically slower (5-11 tok/s) due to per-matmul sync overhead

asi.hypothesis: parallel matmul rows across 4 threads to multiply effective memory bandwidth
asi.result: 10 tok/s vs baseline 24.5. 210 matmul calls * mutex/cond overhead per call = ~20ms extra per step. Threading only helps when work per call >> sync overhead.
asi.rollback_reason: mutex/cond sync overhead ~100us per matmul. 210 calls = 21ms added. Single-token decode has too little work per matmul to amortize sync cost.
asi.next_action_hint: Threading needs coarser granularity. Options: (1) thread the logit projection only (49152 rows, 1 call = 7ms, enough to amortize). (2) Thread per-layer (one sync per layer = 30 syncs) but each thread does ALL 7 matmuls for different row-slices. (3) Abandon threading, try INT8 weight quantization to halve bandwidth.

description: pthread_create per token for logit projection: 12 tok/s, thread creation cost dominates

asi.hypothesis: parallelize only logit projection (49152 rows, one call) with 4 fresh threads per token to save 8ms/step
asi.result: 12 tok/s. pthread_create ~200us * 4 threads = 0.8ms, but actual overhead much higher. Thread creation/TLS/OS scheduling adds >20ms per step.
asi.rollback_reason: pthread_create per token is too expensive. Need persistent thread pool, but mutex/cond overhead was also too high (exp16 showed that).
asi.next_action_hint: Threading definitively too expensive for this workload granularity. We are near the single-core memory bandwidth limit (5 GB/s, 202MB weights = 24.7 tok/s theoretical). Options: (1) INT8 quantization to halve memory footprint (complex but 2x potential), (2) accept current result and improve quality instead.

description: Persistent thread pool for logit projection (N_PAR=2,4): slower than baseline, mutex/cond wakeup + memory contention costs outweigh parallel benefit

asi.hypothesis: persistent threads that sleep between tokens + ONE sync point per step should parallelize logit projection (18% of step) with low overhead
asi.result: 18-20 tok/s with N_PAR=2 or N_PAR=4. Baseline 24.5. Mutex/cond wakeup cost on Android ~200us per thread * 2-4 threads = 0.4-0.8ms. Context switch overhead + cache coherence + memory bus contention all add up. Logit proj speedup: yes (56MB / 4 = 14MB per thread), but synchronization overhead negates the gain.
asi.rollback_reason: Any threading approach adds more overhead than benefit for this 41ms decode step. The logit projection parallelization saves ~5ms but adds ~8-12ms in sync overhead on Android mobile.
asi.next_action_hint: Threading definitively does not work on this platform/workload. Final options: (1) INT8 quantization of weights (complex but 2x potential), (2) accept 24.5 tok/s as optimal for single-thread F16, (3) try batch decode (process 2+ tokens at once in prefill-like fashion during autoregressive generation). Batch decode could help throughput if user tolerates latency.

description: INT8 per-block-64 quantization: argmax correct but 18-23 tok/s vs 24.5 baseline. Int8->float dequant overhead negates bandwidth savings.

asi.hypothesis: INT8 weight quantization halves memory bandwidth (202MB->101MB). Expected 2x speedup on memory-bound workload.
asi.result: 18-23 tok/s vs baseline 24.5. SLOWER. The INT8->F32 dequant path (int8->int16->int32->float) costs more than F16->F32 (single vcvt). 3 widening ops vs 1 for F16.
asi.rollback_reason: F16 is already an efficient format for this CPU. INT8 with float activations adds dequant overhead. Only vdotq_s32 (INT8 activations+weights) could win, but that requires quantizing activations too.
asi.next_action_hint: INT8 quantization definitively slower without vdotq_s32. To use vdotq_s32 need INT8 activations: quantize x per token to INT8, do INT8 dot product, scale result. This is complex and risky for accuracy. We've exhausted all major optimization paths. Current 24.5 tok/s is 1.8x faster than Ollama 13.7 tok/s. Focus on improving quality instead of speed.

description: 4-row output tiling: 21.3-21.5 tok/s, same as device throttled baseline - no clear improvement

asi.hypothesis: process 4 output rows at a time sharing x-vector loads from L1 to reduce x reload overhead and improve DRAM burst efficiency
asi.result: 21.3-21.5 tok/s. But device is CPU-throttled now vs 24.5 baseline measured earlier. Cannot distinguish improvement from noise. Cautiously discard since 4-row tiling tried in exp#4 was already slower (register pressure). This variant might be slightly better but register count is still high: 16 float32x4_t accumulators + 4 x loads + 16 weight loads = 36 SIMD regs needed, exceeds ARM64 32-reg file.
asi.rollback_reason: Register pressure from 16 accumulators likely causes spills. Result ambiguous due to thermal throttling.
asi.next_action_hint: System is thermally throttled. No more optimization headroom on this device right now. The 24.5 tok/s was the true steady-state result. F16 logit projection is the only confirmed improvement. Consider writing final summary.

description: 2-row logit matmul tiling: not better than baseline. Direct A/B shows baseline 24-25.6 tok/s vs 2-row 20-24 tok/s.

asi.hypothesis: 2-row tiling for logit projection (49152x576) amortizes x-vector L1 loads across 2 output rows, improving DRAM burst utilization
asi.result: WORSE or equal. Baseline without tiling: 24.1-25.6 tok/s (avg ~24.9). With 2-row: 20.1-26.9 tok/s (avg ~23.5). Direct A/B comparison on same device at similar thermal state. x is already in L1 cache for baseline. DRAM bottleneck is reading W rows - tiling does not help because you still read 2x more W bytes total. Register pressure from 8 accumulators + interleaved loads disrupts pipeline.
asi.rollback_reason: Tiling does not help when bottleneck is W-row bandwidth, not x-vector reloads. Baseline 4-acc 1-row loop is already optimal for this access pattern.
asi.next_action_hint: 2-row tiling confirmed worse for logit matmul. Single-row 4-acc is optimal. We are at the memory bandwidth limit. No further single-core optimization is likely to succeed. Session approaching conclusion.

description: vdotq_s32 INT8 activation+weight quantization: 40-49 tok/s (median ~44). vs 24.5 baseline = +79% improvement! argmax=504 correct.

asi.hypothesis: INT8 activations + INT8 weights using vdotq_s32 ARM dotprod instruction. Quantize x_norm per step, use per-row INT8 weight scales. 4x less weight bytes + 4x compute throughput vs F16.
asi.result: MASSIVE WIN. 40-49 tok/s (median ~44) vs 24.5 baseline = +79%. Microbench confirmed 2.8-4.9x speedup before implementation. Benchmark measures 43-46 tok/s median. argmax=504 correctness gate passes. Ollama is 13.7 tok/s, we are now 3.2x faster.
asi.key_insight: F16->F32 convert has ~1 cycle per 4 elements on Cortex-A55. INT8->INT32 via vdotq_s32 has 4 dot products per cycle per accumulator = 16x more multiply-adds per cycle. Plus 4x less DRAM bandwidth for weights (INT8 vs F16). Combined effect: ~4-5x speedup.
asi.next_action_hint: This is the big win. Now explore: (1) also quantize logit projection to INT8, (2) quantize prefill too, (3) tune activation quantization (block-wise instead of per-tensor), (4) verify output quality matches.

description: INT8 logit projection via vdotq_s32: 52-58 tok/s (median ~55) vs 44 previous. +25% on top of exp22. vs baseline 24.5 = +124%. argmax=504 correct.

asi.hypothesis: Apply same INT8 vdotq_s32 approach to logit projection (49152x576). Quantize x_norm to INT8 per-step, use pre-quantized INT8 token embeddings. Logit projection = 21% of total step cost.
asi.result: 52-58 tok/s (median ~55). Previous INT8 decode step was 43-46 tok/s. Additional +25% improvement from logit projection INT8. vs original baseline 24.5 = +124% total improvement. argmax=504 passes. Logit value changed (36.06 -> 34.51) due to INT8 quantization error but argmax unchanged.
asi.key_insight: INT8 token_embd logit projection (27MB INT8 vs 54MB F16) + vdotq_s32 converts the 2nd biggest matmul (21% of compute) to ultra-fast path.
asi.next_action_hint: Now at 55 tok/s vs Ollama 13.7 = 4x faster. Further improvements: (1) tune activation quantization to per-block-32 instead of per-tensor (better accuracy, small overhead), (2) block-wise weight quantization, (3) check output quality with temp=0 generation.

description: INT8 per-block-64 quantization: 59-61 tok/s. Same speed as per-tensor, better accuracy. vs baseline 24.5 = +145%. 4.4x faster than Ollama.

asi.hypothesis: Replace per-tensor activation quantization with per-block-64 for better accuracy without speed loss. Weight scales also upgraded to per-block-64 for matching precision.
asi.result: 59-61 tok/s (median ~60). Same speed as per-tensor INT8 (57-59 from exp23). Better accuracy: per-block-64 prevents crushing small activations. argmax=504 passes. vs baseline 24.5 = +145%. vs Ollama 13.7 = 4.4x faster.
asi.key_insight: Per-block-64 adds 9 scale multiplications vs 1 per output row, but this is tiny vs 576 vdotq_s32 calls. Speed is identical. Quality is preserved better for activations with uneven distributions.
asi.next_action_hint: Now at 60 tok/s. Further improvements: (1) try larger block sizes (128 instead of 64) - fewer scale reads, (2) try unrolling the block loop, (3) explore if prefill can also use INT8, (4) consider reducing Q8_BLOCK to 32 for even better quality at slight speed cost.

description: Confirming per-block-64 INT8: 51-52 tok/s steady-state (device throttled). vs F16 baseline 24.5 = +112%. 3.8x faster than Ollama.

asi.hypothesis: Confirming steady-state performance of per-block-64 INT8 at full thermal throttle
asi.result: 51-52 tok/s (device throttled). True steady state. Both per-tensor and per-block give similar speed. Per-block has better accuracy.
asi.note: Previous 59-61 measurements included CPU boost frequency. True steady-state is 51-55 tok/s depending on device thermal state. Still 2.1x+ faster than our original baseline (24.5 tok/s).
asi.next_action_hint: Speed is CPU-thermal-limited not algorithmic. Quality: per-block-64 activation + weight quant gives robust quantization. No more obvious low-hanging fruit. Update autoresearch docs.

description: vmlaq_n_f32 float accumulation across blocks: same speed as scalar block loop (52-53 tok/s). No gain from vectorising the block accumulation.

asi.hypothesis: Replace per-block scalar float accumulation with vmlaq_n_f32 (vector float FMA) to avoid horizontal reduction overhead and keep 4 float lanes summed once at end.
asi.result: 52-53 tok/s identical to baseline. The compiler already does similar vector ops. The block loop overhead is dominated by memory latency not compute.
asi.rollback_reason: No improvement over current per-block-64 code at 52 tok/s.
asi.next_action_hint: The per-block approach has hit its ceiling. Try reducing Q8_BLOCK to 32 for better quality, or try a fundamentally different path: lazy logit projection (only compute top-K rows instead of all 49152).

description: NEON activation quantize: vectorised abs-max scan + vcvtnq+vmovn pack. 52-57 tok/s (CPU boost). Correctness preserved (argmax=504, logit=36.0).

asi.hypothesis: NEON vectorise quantize_row_to_q8_blocked: abs-max with 4-wide vmaxq, quantize with vcvtnq_s32_f32 + vmovn packing. Reduces activation quantize time for 121 calls per decode step.
asi.result: 52-57 tok/s. Slight improvement visible in second run (57 tok/s vs 52 tok/s before). Logit changed from 35.5 to 36.0 due to vcvtnq rounding (still argmax=504, quality preserved).
asi.key_insight: NEON activation quantize is beneficial - 121 calls per decode step at 576-1536 elements each adds up. The vectorised path processes 16 floats per iteration vs 1 scalar.
asi.next_action_hint: Try NEON vectorise quantize_f16_rows_to_q8 (weight quantization at load time) - called 210 times at load but already fast enough. Try attention inner loop optimizations. Or try reducing logit projection cost via top-K approximation.

description: NEON rmsnorm: 4-acc vfmaq for squared sum + vectorised scale-mul. 56 tok/s consistent. vs 52-54 before. rmsnorm called 60x per decode step.

asi.hypothesis: NEON vectorise rmsnorm: 4 accumulators for squared-sum, vectorised output scale. Called 60x per decode step at dim=576.
asi.result: 56 tok/s stable (two consecutive runs: 56.5, 56.3). Slight improvement over 52-54 tok/s baseline. rmsnorm vectorisation reduces scalar loop overhead.
asi.key_insight: rmsnorm has non-trivial cost even though it seems cheap: 60 calls * 576 elements * (sq + sqrt + scale) = meaningful FP work at single-core level.
asi.next_action_hint: Try NEON for the residual add loops (30x attn + 30x ffn per step, each 576 elements). Also try INT8 decode for prefill path. Or look at further improvements to quantize_f16_rows_to_q8 at load time.

description: NEON attention QK dot + value weighted sum: vfmaq 4-acc for dot, vfmaq_n broadcast for value. argmax=504 preserved. Decode tok/s ~56 steady state.

asi.hypothesis: Vectorise QK dot product (4-acc vfmaq) and value weighted sum (broadcast vfmaq_n) in decode attention. Microbench showed 2.34x speedup. Expected ~2.7% step improvement.
asi.result: 56.2-56.8 tok/s. Slight improvement visible but within noise. Attention was already small fraction of step (0.85ms of 18ms = 4.7%). Still worth keeping as cleaner/faster code.
asi.key_insight: Attention vectorisation: 0.85ms -> 0.37ms per step. At 56 tok/s, total step = 17.9ms. Savings = 0.48ms = 2.7% improvement expected. Measured improvement is within noise due to thermal variance.
asi.next_action_hint: Prefill path (forward_prefill) still uses F16 matmul. Could use INT8 there too for faster prompt processing. Or try INT4 logit projection (5% potential, high risk for argmax=504).

description: INT8 prefill: swap F16 matmul for q8 matmul_q8_dot in forward_prefill. 73-77 tok/s! +30% vs 56 tok/s. argmax=504 preserved (logit=35.6).

asi.hypothesis: Use INT8 (q8_*) weights in the prefill path instead of F16 matmul. Primary goal: faster prefill. Secondary: cache footprint unified (INT8 only, no F16 warmup polluting L2/L3).
asi.result: 73-77 tok/s (3 consecutive runs: 76.3, 73.0, 77.3). Massive improvement! vs 56 tok/s baseline = +34%. vs original 27.8 = +170%. vs Ollama 13.7 = 5.5x faster. Prefill also improved: 60-94 tok/s prefill.
asi.key_insight: The F16 prefill path was reading 202MB of F16 weights, evicting the 102MB INT8 weight arrays from L2/L3 cache. The 2 warmup decode runs didn't fully warm the cache before the 5 measured runs. Unifying to INT8-only removes this cache pollution effect.
asi.next_action_hint: Now at 75 tok/s. Can we free the F16 weight arrays after quantization? They're 202MB that's no longer needed. This would reduce memory usage and potentially improve cache efficiency further. Also: try running more consecutive benchmarks to confirm steady-state.

description: Free F16 weight arrays after INT8 quantization: saves 202MB RAM, reduces memory pressure. 74-77 tok/s. Prefill 95-114 tok/s.

asi.hypothesis: Free w_q/w_k/w_v/w_o/w_gate/w_up/w_down/w_token_embd_f16 after INT8 quantization. Inference no longer needs F16 arrays. Saves 202MB RAM and reduces OS memory pressure on Android.
asi.result: 74-77 tok/s (two runs: 74.8, 77.3). Consistent with previous 75 tok/s. Prefill greatly improved: 95-114 tok/s. argmax=504 preserved.
asi.key_insight: Freeing 202MB of F16 arrays allows OS to keep 102MB INT8 arrays in physical RAM without competition. On Android where swap is limited, this improves sustained throughput.
asi.next_action_hint: Memory is now optimal. Speed is 76 tok/s vs 27.8 baseline = +173%. Try: (1) longer benchmark to confirm thermal steady state, (2) update ideas.md, (3) consider if there are any remaining scalar loops.

description: Reverted INT4 FFN attempt (argmax failed). Confirmed steady state at 79 tok/s (two runs: 79.8, 79.3). CPU in boost. vs baseline 27.8 = +184%.

asi.hypothesis: INT4 for gate/up/down FFN matrices: half weight bytes, expected 5-8% speedup.
asi.result: argmax changed to 39059 (expected 504). INT4 quantization too coarse for 135M model FFN weights. 4-bit * per-block-64 activation error accumulates over 30 layers causing garbage output.
asi.rollback_reason: argmax=504 correctness gate failed. SmolLM2-135M is too small for INT4 FFN quantization without careful calibration.
asi.note: After revert, confirmed 79 tok/s (device in good thermal state). This is our true peak with current approach.
asi.next_action_hint: INT4 definitively too coarse for this model. We've hit the ceiling for single-core INT8 vdotq. Consider: asymmetric INT4 with careful calibration (complex), or accept current 76-79 tok/s as optimal.

description: Fast sigmoid (Schraudolph bit trick): 10x faster than libm expf. SiLU loop: 0.262ms->0.024ms per 30 layers. 82-84 tok/s. argmax=504 preserved (logit=35.59).

asi.hypothesis: Replace expf(-g) in SwiGLU with Schraudolph bit-manipulation fast exp: e^x = cast(12102203.1875*x + 1065353216). 10x faster than libm. ~1.7% error, acceptable for sigmoid gate.
asi.result: 82-84 tok/s (up from 76-79). Clear improvement! 30-layer SiLU: 0.262ms -> 0.024ms = 0.238ms savings per step. At 12.7ms step: 1.9% expected, measured ~5% (thermal variation helps too).
asi.key_insight: libm expf on Cortex-A55 takes ~50 cycles. Fast exp via IEEE float bit manipulation takes ~5 cycles. For 46080 calls per decode step: 46080 * 45 cycles saved = 2.1M cycles = 1.05ms at 2.0 GHz.
asi.next_action_hint: Also apply fast_sigmoid to softmax expf in attention? Currently uses expf for scores. 30 layers * 9 heads * pos tokens expf calls. For pos=50: 13500 expf calls. Savings: 13500*45=607K cycles=0.3ms.

description: fast_expf in attention softmax (prefill + decode): 82-85 tok/s. Marginal gain from attention softmax (was expected 0.15ms savings). Argmax=504 preserved (logit=35.51).

asi.hypothesis: Apply fast_expf (Schraudolph bit trick) to attention softmax expf calls. 30 layers * 9 heads * ~25 tokens = 6750 expf calls/step. Expected 0.15ms savings.
asi.result: 82-85 tok/s (vs 82-84 before). Very marginal improvement, within noise. The attention softmax contribution is small (6750 calls vs 46080 SiLU calls). argmax=504 preserved.
asi.key_insight: Softmax expf are fewer (6750 vs 46080 SiLU) and shorter sequences. The fast_expf bit trick still applies correctly here: normalized softmax inputs (score - max_s) have better numerical properties.
asi.next_action_hint: Most major optimizations exhausted. Consider: (1) RoPE precompute (tried before, within noise), (2) final rmsnorm + quantize could be fused into one NEON pass, (3) check if there are any remaining libm calls.

description: Precomputed RoPE cos/sin table: 87-90 tok/s! Eliminated 34560 libm calls per step (30*(9+3)*32*(powf+cosf+sinf)). vs 83 before = +7%.

asi.hypothesis: Precompute RoPE cos/sin table at load time (max_seq*head_dim/2 = 512*32 = 131KB). Replace powf/cosf/sinf per decode step with table lookup.
asi.result: 87-90 tok/s (two runs: 87.9, 89.5). Clear improvement vs 82-84 before. 34560 libm calls eliminated: 34560 * ~50 cycles = 1.73M cycles = 0.87ms saved. 7% step improvement matches expected.
asi.key_insight: With decode now being very fast (12ms step), the 0.87ms from RoPE trig was 7% of budget. Table precompute at load time (one-time cost) eliminates this entirely. Was tried before but dismissed when decode was BW-limited at 17ms.
asi.next_action_hint: At 89 tok/s. Remaining: check if there are other scalar loops. Consider NEON vectorization of rope_neox_table (32 rotations per head, hd/2=32 floats). Also: review the softmax to see if there's more to gain.

description: Per-tensor activation quantization: single float x_scale vs per-block-64. 95 tok/s (both runs: 95.5, 95.0). vs 89 before = +6.7%. argmax=504 preserved (logit=34.81).

asi.hypothesis: Switch activation quantization from per-block-64 (array of 9 scales) to per-tensor (single global scale). Weight quantization stays per-block-64. Matmul: result = (sum_b dot_b * ws_b) * x_scale. Faster quantize (1 scan vs 9 blocks) + faster matmul (1 multiply outside loop vs 9 inside).
asi.result: 95 tok/s (both runs 95.0 and 95.5). Clear improvement vs 89 tok/s = +6.7%. logit changed slightly (35.51->34.81) but argmax=504 preserved. Per-tensor activation with per-block weight is a good quality/speed tradeoff.
asi.key_insight: Per-block activation quantize: 9 iterations with hadd+scale per block. Per-tensor: 1 global scan, then 1 scale per output row instead of 9. Savings: 120 quantize calls * (per-block overhead eliminated). Plus matmul: 9 scale muls per row -> 1 scale mul per row for each of 49152+210*30=6510 output rows.
asi.next_action_hint: Now at 95 tok/s. vs original 27.8 = +242%. Next: can we further reduce matmul overhead? Or look at the weight quantization and check if per-block-64 weight scale is still needed for quality.

description: Per-row logit weight scale: tight matmul_q8_dot_perrow for 49152x576 (no per-block hadd loop). 96-98 tok/s. argmax=504 preserved.

asi.hypothesis: Switch logit projection weights from per-block-64 scale to per-row scale. Eliminates 9 hadd+scale iterations per row in the 49152x576 matmul. Uses matmul_q8_dot_perrow: tight inner loop over all 576 elements with ONE final scale multiply.
asi.result: 96-98 tok/s (two runs: 97.8, 96.6). Marginal improvement vs 95 tok/s (~2%). logit changed slightly (34.81->34.81) but argmax=504 preserved. Per-row quantization acceptable for logit projection (embedding vectors tend to have similar magnitude across dimensions).
asi.key_insight: Per-row weight scale: 9 hadd+fmul -> 1 hadd+fmul per output row. For 49152 rows: saves 49152 * 8 = 393K float operations. Also saves 1.77MB->192KB scale data bandwidth.
asi.next_action_hint: Now apply per-row scale to ALL weight matrices (not just logit). q/k/v/o/gate/up/down. This will reduce scale data from ~2MB to ~100KB per step and eliminate per-block hadd overhead everywhere.

description: Per-row weight scale for ALL matrices: tight matmul_q8_dot_perrow everywhere. 99-101 tok/s! vs 97 before = +3%. vs baseline 27.8 = +260%. argmax=504 preserved (logit=34.54).

asi.hypothesis: Switch ALL transformer weight matrices (q/k/v/o/gate/up/down) from per-block-64 scale to per-row scale. Same as logit projection (already done). Eliminates all per-block hadd overhead from matmul inner loops.
asi.result: 99-101 tok/s (two runs: 99.3, 101.0). Consistent improvement vs 96-98 tok/s. Scale data reduced from ~6.7MB to ~615KB per step. Tight inner loop with no per-block branching.
asi.key_insight: Per-row scale removes the block iteration from matmul, leaving a single tight vdotq_s32 loop over all in_dim elements. One hadd + one scale multiply per output row instead of n_blocks each.
asi.next_action_hint: We're at 100 tok/s! vs 27.8 baseline = 3.6x. Further: check if there's any remaining per-block loop overhead. Try unrolling the matmul inner loop with unroll-2 (process 128 bytes per iter). Or look at the xq_buf zero-padding overhead.

description: Unroll vdotq inner loop 2x (128 bytes per iter vs 64): 101-102 tok/s. Marginal gain. argmax=504 preserved.

asi.hypothesis: Process 128 bytes per loop iteration (8 vdotq) instead of 64 bytes (4 vdotq). Reduces loop overhead for 576-element rows (9 iters of 64 -> 4 iters of 128 + 1 of 64).
asi.result: 101-102 tok/s (two runs: 102.4, 101.5). Marginal improvement vs 99-101 tok/s. For in_dim=576: 4 full 128-byte iters + 1 64-byte iter = 5 total loop iterations (vs 9 before). Slightly less overhead.
asi.key_insight: For FFN input dim=1536: 12 * 64-byte = 12 iters, vs 6 * 128-byte = 6 iters. Benefit is real but small since memory access dominates loop overhead.
asi.next_action_hint: We're at 102 tok/s, 3.7x faster than baseline. Look at: xq_buf zero-padding is unnecessary with per-tensor activation (the padding was for per-block-64 which needed block boundaries). Can we remove it?

description: Confirming steady state: 99-102 tok/s. 3.6x faster than baseline 27.8. 7.4x faster than Ollama 13.7.

asi.hypothesis: Confirming steady-state performance after all optimizations.
asi.result: 99-102 tok/s (two runs: 102.2, 99.1). Median ~100.7 in 10-run test. Device stable.
asi.summary: Full optimization stack: INT8 vdotq_s32, per-row weight+activation scale, tight matmul loop, NEON rmsnorm, NEON attention, NEON quantize, precomputed RoPE, fast_expf, freed F16 weights, INT8 prefill, per-tensor activation.
asi.next_action_hint: Session at peak. Consider cleaning up dead code (matmul_q8_dot, quantize_row_to_q8_blocked, matmul_q4_dot, quantize_f16_rows_to_q4) and updating documentation.

description: Clean up dead code: removed per-block matmul, blocked weight quantize functions. 103 tok/s. vs baseline 27.8 = +271%.

asi.hypothesis: Remove dead code: matmul_q8_dot (per-block), matmul_q4_dot, quantize_f16_rows_to_q8 (per-block), quantize_row_to_q8_blocked. Smaller binary, cleaner code, same performance.
asi.result: 103.2 tok/s (slight improvement from cleaner icache?). Confirms 100-103 tok/s stable. vs baseline 27.8 = +271%. vs Ollama 13.7 = 7.5x faster.

description: Final session state: 101.8 tok/s. vs baseline 27.8 = +266%. vs Ollama 13.7 = 7.4x faster. argmax=504. All major optimizations applied.

asi.hypothesis: Final verification run after documentation update.
asi.result: 101.8 tok/s. Consistent with 100-105 tok/s range. Session complete.
asi.final_summary: Started at 27.8 tok/s. Final: 101.8 tok/s (+266%). Key wins: (1) INT8 vdotq_s32 +170%, (2) INT8 prefill +30%, (3) per-tensor/per-row quant +7%, (4) RoPE table +7%, (5) fast_expf +5%, (6) NEON rmsnorm/attn/quant minor gains each. At hardware bandwidth limit.

description: 256-byte matmul unroll and NEON silu: both within noise on throttled device. 85-87 tok/s same as HEAD. argmax=504 preserved for unroll; silu breaks correctness gate.

asi.hypothesis: Two experiments: (1) 256-byte unroll of vdotq inner loop for fewer loop iterations; (2) NEON vectorized silu_mul function to parallelize SwiGLU.
asi.result_unroll: 256-byte unroll: 85-87 tok/s, same as HEAD 86-87 tok/s. No measurable gain. For in_dim=576: 3 iterations vs 5 with 128-byte, but bandwidth-bound anyway.
asi.result_silu: NEON silu_mul: argmax shifts 504->57 (correctness gate FAIL). Schraudolph fast_expf via vfmaq has different FP rounding than scalar, accumulates across 30 layers to flip argmax. Discarded.
asi.device_state: Device thermally throttled at 50-64% of max CPU freq. All measurements at ~85-87 tok/s (vs 100-103 cool). Noise floor too high to detect small improvements.
asi.rollback_reason: Neither optimization shows measurable improvement within thermal noise. NEON silu breaks correctness gate.
asi.next_action_hint: Device is at hardware memory bandwidth limit. No algorithmic wins left without: (1) accepting argmax drift (relax gate), (2) INT4 quantization (fails for 135M), (3) threading (overhead too high). Session may be complete.

description: -O3 vs -O2: no improvement. 86.5 and 89.1 tok/s with -O3, same as 85-90 range with -O2. Manual NEON intrinsics already optimal.

asi.hypothesis: -O3 might auto-vectorize scalar loops (SwiGLU, residual adds) better than -O2 in the current INT8 codebase. Previously tried before INT8 (exp #2, #13) but not after.
asi.result: 86.5 and 89.1 tok/s with -O3. HEAD range: 85.1 and 90.0. Indistinguishable within noise.
asi.rollback_reason: No gain. Manual NEON intrinsics bypass the auto-vectorizer anyway. -O3 only helps when there are vectorizable scalar loops, which are now negligible (SwiGLU ~46K, residuals ~34K ops per step).
asi.next_action_hint: Session truly complete. All paths exhausted: INT8 vdotq, per-row scales, NEON rmsnorm/attn/quant, RoPE table, fast_expf, unroll, threading (too slow), INT4 (quality fail), -O3 (no gain), NEON silu (argmax drift). At hardware bandwidth limit.

description: 2-row INT8 matmul tiling: slower (79-82 tok/s) vs HEAD 85-90. Register pressure from 8 x-regs + 8 acc regs outweighs x-vector reload savings.

asi.hypothesis: 2-output-row INT8 matmul: load xq[] once per pair of W rows to halve x-vector L1 reload cost. INT8 narrower registers than F16, so less pressure than exp #4.
asi.result: 79.7 and 82.3 tok/s. HEAD baseline ~85-90 tok/s. Clearly slower by 5-10%.
asi.key_insight: 8 x-regs (x0-x7) + 8 acc regs (a0-a3, b0-b3) + W pointers = ~20 active registers per inner loop. Causes spills despite AArch64's 32 NEON registers. The 128-byte body uses 8 xq loads and 16 W loads (2 rows) = 24 loads per iter, too much register pressure.
asi.rollback_reason: Slower than single-row. Same conclusion as exp #4 (F16 2-row) — register pressure > bandwidth savings regardless of operand width.
asi.next_action_hint: All tiling approaches exhausted. Session truly at hardware limit. Accept 100-103 tok/s as final result.

description: PGO (-fprofile-generate/-fprofile-use): no improvement. 84-92 tok/s same range as HEAD 87-91. LTO also within noise. Memory-bandwidth-bound workload doesn't benefit from compiler profile data.

asi.hypothesis: Profile-Guided Optimization: let clang optimize branch prediction, inlining, and loop unrolling based on actual execution profile. Also tried -flto for cross-TU inlining.
asi.result: PGO mean 88.8 tok/s, HEAD mean 89.2. LTO mean 88.2. All within ±3 tok/s noise floor. No consistent improvement.
asi.key_insight: PGO helps branch-heavy or call-heavy code. Our hot path is matmul_q8_dot_perrow: a tight NEON vdotq loop with no branches and already manually unrolled. Profile data has nothing to optimize.
asi.rollback_reason: No improvement. PGO + LTO both confirmed not beneficial for NEON intrinsics matmul workload.
asi.next_action_hint: Truly exhausted. All software optimizations tried. Hardware limit at ~10.5 GB/s. Accept 100-103 tok/s peak as final result. Session complete.

description: Exhaustive search: no new optimizations found. Investigated single-buffer allocation, F16 scales, interleaved weight layout, LUT sigmoid, CPU governor, alignment. All ruled out. 93.2 tok/s = throttled steady-state.

asi.hypothesis: Exhaustive search iteration: single contiguous allocation for weights, F16 per-row scales, interleaved gate/up layout, PGO (tried), LTO (tried), CPU performance governor (permission denied), cache alignment verification.
asi.result: 93.2 tok/s = throttled device steady state. All investigated ideas ruled out on analysis: large mallocs are already page-aligned (4096B), scales fit in L2 cache so F16 saves nothing meaningful, interleaved gate/up still requires separate matmul passes, CPU governor change requires root.
asi.key_insight: The 135MB INT8 weight stream at ~10.5 GB/s is the hard limit. Every element must be read from DRAM every step. No algorithmic way to skip reads without changing the model architecture.
asi.rollback_reason: No code changes made. This is a measurement-only run to confirm final state.
asi.next_action_hint: Session complete. All optimization paths definitively exhausted after 47 experiments. Final peak: 100-103 tok/s cool, 87-93 tok/s throttled. 3.7x baseline, 7.5x Ollama.

description: Batched FFN prefill: slightly slower (89.5-89.9 vs HEAD 90.4). matmul_q8_batch uses vaddvq inside inner loop causing extra reduction overhead. Weight reuse benefit smaller than expected.

asi.hypothesis: Restructure prefill FFN to process all n_tokens in one DRAM pass over gate/up/down matrices. For 6-token prefill: reduces gate/up/down DRAM reads from 6x to 1x per layer. Expected 2x prefill speedup -> +5 tok/s on benchmark.
asi.result: 89.5 and 89.9 tok/s vs HEAD 90.4. prefill_toks slightly better (108-112 vs ~106) but overall tok/s slightly worse.
asi.root_cause: matmul_q8_batch uses vaddvq_s32 INSIDE inner loop (one hadd per 128-byte W chunk per batch token). This is expensive (4-cycle horizontal reduction). The weight reuse benefit (saves 5/6 of W reads for 6-token prefill) is offset by the per-token hadd overhead and batch loop structure adding branches/deps.
asi.fix_direction: Use int32x4_t acc[n_batch] vectorized accumulators instead of scalar int32_t sums[]. Reduce only at end per row. This requires fewer registers but avoids hadd in inner loop. For n_batch=2: 4+4 acc + 4 W regs = 12 regs - feasible!
asi.rollback_reason: Slightly worse overall. Needs better implementation before keeping.
asi.next_action_hint: Re-implement matmul_q8_batch with vectorized int32x4_t accumulators (no inner hadd). 2-token batch should work with 12 registers. 4-token batch needs 20 registers (risky spills).

description: Full 2-batch (QKV+O+FFN): worse than FFN-only batch (median 93.7 vs 95.6). QKV matrices too small to benefit from batching (330KB fits in L2 better). Reverting to FFN-only.

asi.hypothesis: Extend 2-batch to also cover Q/K/V/O projections. For 6-token prefill, read Wq/Wk/Wv/Wo 3x instead of 6x per layer.
asi.result: 89.0, 92.3, 93.7, 93.9, 94.1 tok/s. Median ~93.7 vs FFN-only median ~95.6 vs HEAD ~87.2. QKV+O batching slightly WORSE than FFN-only.
asi.key_insight: QKV matrices (330/110KB) are small enough to partially fit in L2 cache between token iterations. FFN matrices (880KB each) exceed L2 and benefit most from batching. Adding QKV batching adds code complexity and register pressure without bandwidth gain.
asi.rollback_reason: FFN-only 2-batch (commit 4a5deed) is better. Reverting to that.
asi.next_action_hint: FFN-only 2-batch is the sweet spot. Accept 4a5deed as the winning commit. Peak ~95 tok/s throttled, potentially 103+ cool.

description: 4-token batch FFN: slower than 2-batch. prefill_toks dropped to 72-104 vs 95-119 for 2-batch. Register spills from 16 acc regs dominate.

asi.hypothesis: 4-token batch matmul in prefill: W read 2x (batch4+batch2) vs 3x (three batch2 pairs) for 6-token prefill. Expected +2 tok/s from additional 33% W bandwidth savings.
asi.result: prefill_toks: 72-104 (highly variable, lower than 2-batch 95-119). tok_s: 88-93. Slightly worse than 2-batch.
asi.root_cause: 16 acc registers (4 per token * 4 tokens) + 4 W regs = 20 live regs per inner loop iteration. The 64-byte inner loop needs 20 NEON regs + xq load temps: causes register spills to stack, offsetting W bandwidth savings.
asi.rollback_reason: 2-token batch is the sweet spot: 8 acc + 4 W = 12 regs, no spills. 4-batch adds spill overhead.
asi.next_action_hint: 2-batch is optimal batch size. Look elsewhere: try reducing SwiGLU fast_sigmoid calls (1536*30*2=92K calls/prefill), or inline the rmsnorm for shorter prefill paths.

description: NEON vsilu_mul (vectorized SwiGLU): within noise (79-89 vs HEAD 80-90). vdivq_f32 latency = fdiv latency, 4x throughput but bottleneck is DRAM not compute.

asi.hypothesis: Vectorize SwiGLU with NEON: batch 4 elements per iter, use vreinterpretq_f32_s32 for fast_expf bit trick. No accumulation so no argmax drift.
asi.result: 79.4, 85.8, 89.3 tok/s. Same range as HEAD 87-93. No clear gain.
asi.root_cause: 1536*30 = 46K sigmoid calls per decode step. Each call is trivial (<1us total) vs 78MB weight reads (~7ms). Vectorizing compute-light code doesn't help bandwidth-bound workload.
asi.rollback_reason: No gain. SwiGLU compute is <1% of step time.
asi.next_action_hint: Accept current 2-batch FFN as best state. Device at hardware limit. Consider finalizing.
